text: JavaScript for ServiceNow Developers introduced Script Includes as reusable server-side code, callable from Business Rules, Client Scripts, and other scripts. What that course didn't cover is how the platform actually loads that code behind the scenes, and why that loading model matters once a real instance accumulates thousands of these things over the years.

Take this line, running inside a Business Rule: new ApprovalUtils, followed by a call to isApprover, passing in the current user and the current record. Before that line executes anywhere on the instance, ApprovalUtils is nothing but a row of text sitting in the sys_script_include table. It isn't parsed. It isn't compiled. It's simply stored, exactly like any other database record, waiting.

That's the key distinction worth internalizing: Script Includes are lazy-loaded, not eagerly loaded. At instance startup, nothing happens to any of them — no parsing, no compiling, no memory allocated, no measurable cost whatsoever. Only on that first real call does the platform compile the script and cache the compiled result in memory, so every later call on that same node reuses the cached version instead of recompiling from scratch each time.

This is exactly why a large, mature instance can carry thousands of Script Includes with zero performance cost from the ones nobody happens to call during a given transaction. It's also why experienced developers don't hesitate to split logic into a new, narrowly-scoped Script Include rather than overloading an existing one — there's genuinely no startup tax either way you choose to organize it. One more field worth knowing about now, even if only at a glance: Accessible from, set to either all application scopes or this application scope only. We're only previewing that concept here; the real cross-scope access rules get their own full treatment in Chapter 5.

Lazy loading is the real reason Script Include count simply isn't a performance worry on real-world instances, no matter how many accumulate over the years. Next, Lesson 12 breaks down the actual class-based pattern professional ServiceNow developers write with Class.create, piece by piece, starting with what that call really returns.
